blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: We present minimal solvers for joint homography and radial distortion estimation using affine- or orientation-covariant features. The core contribution is a set of novel constraints that exploit local feature geometry inherent to affine descriptors, enabling solvers that require fewer correspondences than point-based methods. Using modern robust estimation frameworks, we demonstrate that the proposed solvers are advantageous to the current state-of-the-art with a significant speed-up in the presence of outliers while maintaining comparable or superior estimation accuracy. The proposed solvers are tested on both synthetic and real images containing challenging fisheye distortions.
blocks.zh: 我们提出最低限度的解析器,用于利用亲缘或定向的共变特征进行联合的同位素和射线扭曲估计。 核心贡献是一套新颖的制约因素,它们利用affine描述符所固有的局部特征几何,使得需要比点法更少的函证的解析器成为可能. 我们利用现代强力估计框架,表明提议的解决者对目前的先进水平是有利的,在有外部因素的情况下可以大大加快速度,同时保持可比或较高的估计准确性。 提议的解决者在合成和真实的图像上都经过测试,这些图像含有挑战性的鱼眼扭曲。

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
For more than twenty years [ 26 ] affine features have been used in geometric computer vision applications.
Early work includes [ 31 ] , where it was shown how to estimate the epipolar geometry of an
uncalibrated pair of cameras from two correspondences of local affine frames (LAFs). Since then, there have been numerous methods that exploit their intrinsically encoded properties.
Recent work include homography estimation [ 1 ] ,
relative pose estimation [ 2 , 14 , 18 ] ,
including partially calibrated cameras [ 20 ] and
generalized relative pose [ 17 ] , as well as the
absolute pose problem [ 44 ] .

blocks.en:
The main theoretical advantage of leveraging affine features in epipolar geometry is the smaller sample size needed in the resulting solver, thus requiring fewer RANSAC iterations in order to to draw an all-inlier subset. The main criticism against using affine solvers has been that they have not been working well in practice; however, Barath et al . [ 5 ] provided a framework for improving affine solvers for various camera geometry estimation pipelines, making them robust and reliable for real-world data. Another issue,
raised in e.g . , [ 38 ] , is the added computational time for extracting the affine features themselves.
To avoid this computational overhead,
Barath and Kukelova [ 3 ] showed how scale- and orientation-covariant features can be interpreted
as local affine features, utilizing the intrinsic geometric properties of the feature descriptors, thus providing more local information than the point correspondences alone, while not having to compute the affine features explicitly.
They derived a set of constraints characterizing the relationship between affine feature descriptors and the scale- and orientation-covariant counterpart, from which they constructed a
homography solver requiring only two scale- and orientation-covariant features. Ding et al . showed how to incorporate a known
reference direction [ 11 ] from an IMU using these constraints and further assumptions on the plane normals ( e.g . , vertical and horizontal walls).
In [ 4 ] , scale- and orientation-covariant features were used for general problems in epipolar
geometry. This was later used for the application of autonomous driving in [ 38 ] , where upright essential
matrices were estimated with great computational improvement compared to point-based and affine-based methods. Ventura et al . [ 45 ] derived new constraints for the absolute pose problem from two oriented features and the upright case (using IMU data) from a single scale- and orientation-covariant feature.
Barath [ 6 ] further showed how to leverage any affine-based solver by approximating affine features directly from
scale- and orientation-covariant features.

blocks.en:
Homography estimation is at the core of many computer vision applications, e.g . , the famous camera calibration method
implemented in OpenCV and many other frameworks, known as Zhang’s method [ 51 ] , where a planar calibration target with a
checkerboard pattern is placed at different positions in the field-of-view of the camera. Even in the era of deep learning,
homography estimation has not become obsolete, but instead been incorporated as geometric priors [ 23 , 9 , 50 ] .
Due to the computational efficiency of state-of-the-art methods for homography estimation, it is integrated in many
modern augmented reality (AR) and mixed reality (MR) platforms, and plays a crucial part for localizing planar surfaces on such devices. Early examples of how to
place augmented objects on and subsequently interact with them include [ 36 , 52 ] .
Recently, Nakano [ 30 ] argued that the one-sided radial distortion homography estimation case is more interesting
for AR/MR applications as one image is often anchored in 3D space thus unaffected (or already corrected for) lens distortion artifacts, see Fig. 1 . Another common scenario
for this setup is in cases of relocalization in an existing environment, where the 3D reconstruction has been corrected for distortion artifacts, but the current intrinsic parameters of the devices are unknown. Failure to accurately account for distortion artifacts in such scenarios greatly reduces the homography estimations and the subsequent placement of objects, lowering the quality of the overall user experience.

blocks.en: In this paper, we consider homography estimation using affine features of radially distorted images. Our core contributions consist of the following: • Theoretical justification and novel geometric constraints for one-sided radially distorted homographies from affine-covariant features and orientation-covariant features, • Fast and accurate geometric solvers utilizing these new constraints, which are capable of using minimal and non-minimal samples, making it suitable for integration in modern robust estimation frameworks, • Comparison to the state-of-the-art methods on synthetic and real data, where the proposed solvers are shown to be faster than traditional point-based solvers while maintaining the same level of accuracy.

blocks.en:
A homography 𝖧 \mathsf{H} , also known as projective transformation, between two point correspondences 𝒙 1 ↔ 𝒙 2 \bm{x}_{1}\leftrightarrow\bm{x}_{2} , where 𝒙 1 = [ u 1 , v 1 , 1 ] T \bm{x}_{1}=[u_{1},\,v_{1},\,1]^{T} and 𝒙 2 = [ u 2 , v 2 , 1 ] T \bm{x}_{2}=[u_{2},\,v_{2},\,1]^{T} , respectively, obeys the relationship 𝒙 2 ∼ 𝖧 ​ 𝒙 1 \bm{x}_{2}\sim{\mathsf{H}}\bm{x}_{1} ,
where ∼ \sim denotes equality up to scale.
In order to estimate a homography in the general case, one requires at least four point correspondences—two constraints are
given for each point correspondences and there are in total eight degrees of freedom, since the homography is only determined up to scale. A classic algorithm for estimating the homography is the direct linear transformation (DLT) [ 19 ] . If additional information is known, the number of degrees of freedom may be reduced, and the geometric
information encoded into the governing equations, thus reducing the number of necessary image correspondences. This can be
achieved by mechanically constraining the camera [ 25 , 46 , 47 , 48 , 39 , 40 , 41 ] which can be extended to the two cameras connected by a rigid body motion [ 37 ] .
If known, a common reference direction can be used, which can be either obtained by mechanical alignment or by utilizing inertial
measurement units (IMUs) to obtain the gravity
direction [ 35 , 13 , 43 ] .
Affine features add additional knowledge of the scene, and have been used directly [ 1 ] or approximated
from scale- and orientation-covariant features [ 10 ] , where the latter require only a single feature in
order to estimate the homography.

blocks.en:
Despite its recent popularity, affine features have not been used extensively in estimating lens distortion. One reason
for this might be that distortion affects the entire image, thus acting globally, and the local nature of affine features
are thought to not encoded such phenomena accurately.
The work by Pritts et al . [ 32 , 33 ] stands alone in addressing this subject. They proposed a set of solvers to
jointly undistort and affinely-rectified an image based on translation directions of coplanar repeated scene texture.
This is done by utilizing that an affine-rectifying homography transforms the image of the vanishing
line of the scene plane to the line at infinity. While demonstrating the feasibility of using affine-covariant features to estimate
lens distortions, the method does not estimate the homography between two images and makes specific assumptions on the scene
geometry by requiring repeated patterns.

blocks.en:
We compare our proposed solvers to the classic solver by Fitzgibbon [ 15 ] , and two recent ones by Nakano [ 30 ] and Wadenbäck et al . [ 49 ] . These all consider the one-sided homography case and rely on point-based correspondences, for which they need 5 (or 4.5) correspondences in the minimal case. Note that in [ 15 ] , only the two-sided case was treated; however, in [ 30 ] it was shown how to apply it to the one-sided case.
All solvers are implemented in C++ using Eigen. The results and timings are done on a standard laptop equipped with a 11th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i5-1145G7 @2.60GHz CPU. Since our method adapts the approach from [ 30 ] , modifying only the coefficients of a matrix in the governing equations, the computational times remain comparable.

blocks.en: 6 Conclusions
blocks.zh: 6. 结论

blocks.en: We have presented new minimal solvers for simultaneous homography and radial distortion estimation leveraging affine- or orientation-covariant features. This efficiently reduces the minimally required sample sizes compared to point-based methods, leading to significantly faster solvers of up to 5 × 5\times the state-of-the-art for point-based solvers. The affine-based solver demonstrates robust performance, achieving excellent homography accuracy and competitive distortion estimation. Its minimal sample size provides a decisive efficiency advantage in RANSAC, enabling faster and more reliable estimation in high-outlier scenarios. While the orientation-covariant solver is more noise-sensitive, it establishes the utility of this feature class for minimal solving. Real-world experiments on fisheye images confirm that both solvers match the accuracy of state-of-the-art methods while being significantly faster, proving their practical value for applications like AR/MR and photogrammetry.
blocks.zh: 我们提出了新的最低解析器,用于同时进行同位素和射线扭曲估计,利用近缘或定向的相通特征。 这与点基方法相比,高效地减少了最低要求的取样大小,使取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取 基于亲缘的解析器表现出了强劲的性能,实现了出色的同位素精度和竞争性扭曲估计. 其最小的样本规模为RANSAC提供了决定性的效率优势,有利于在高输出情景中更快和更可靠的估计. 虽然取向-相变解器对噪声更为敏感,但它确立了这个特性类对最小解的效用. 鱼眼影像上的现实世界实验证实,两种解析器都符合最先进的方法的精度,同时显著地更快,证明了其对AR/MR和相片测量等应用的实用价值.
